title: What Burst can and cannot compile
sub: HPC# without managed objects, strings in Debug.Log, and why throw crashes a player build
cards/0/body:
Burst generates native code that has no garbage collector and no .NET runtime. Hence the main rule of HPC#: no managed objects — nothing that lives on the managed heap.

Not allowed:
— classes and any reference types, List<T> and Dictionary included;
— managed arrays T[] (the exception is a static readonly array that you only read directly: Burst copies it at compile time);
— strings as values, string methods, char and decimal;
— delegates and lambdas;
— boxing: casting a struct to object or to an interface creates a heap object;
— virtual calls — they need a class instance;
— catch (while try/finally and using do work);
— writes to ordinary static fields.

Burst reports such code as a compile error in the console, pointing at the line.
cards/1/body:
Every ban has a Burst-friendly replacement:

— structs instead of classes;
— native containers instead of arrays and collections: NativeArray<T>, NativeList<T>, NativeHashMap and the rest of the Collections package;
— Unity.Mathematics — float3, float4x4, the math.* functions: Burst knows these types and vectorizes them well;
— pointers and unsafe code, stackalloc for a small scratch buffer on the stack;
— FixedString32Bytes, FixedString64Bytes, FixedString128Bytes — a fixed-capacity string stored right inside the struct;
— FunctionPointer<T> instead of a delegate;
— SharedStatic<T> instead of a mutable static field.

System.Math, Interlocked and try/finally also work.
cards/2/q: Match the managed code with its Burst replacement.
cards/3/body:
Burst has no strings as values, but two string features do work — and interviewers like to ask about them.

Debug.Log, Debug.LogWarning and Debug.LogError accept a string literal or an interpolated $"..." (and string.Format) with a literal template. Arguments may only be built-in value types (int, float, bool…) and Unity.Mathematics vectors. Burst builds the message itself, with no managed string.

A literal or the same kind of interpolation can be assigned to a FixedString. What you cannot do is pass a string to your own method, keep it in a struct field, concatenate with + or call ToString() — those are methods of a managed object.
cards/4/q: Which of these will Burst compile? Pick all that apply.
cards/4/options/1: try/finally around work with a buffer
cards/4/options/2: A static readonly int[] table that is only read directly
cards/4/options/4: A string name field in a job struct
cards/4/explain: Interpolation with a primitive in Debug.Log is supported, so is try/finally, and Burst copies a static readonly array at compile time. catch is not supported, a string field is a managed object, and object o = myStruct is boxing, which means a heap object.
cards/5/task: Make DamageJob Burst-compatible: damage becomes NativeArray<float>, crits becomes NativeArray<int> (both are only read, so mark them [ReadOnly]), and the log uses $"..." interpolation with the number instead of string concatenation and ToString().
cards/5/checks/2/label: No managed T[] arrays and no List<T>
cards/5/checks/4/label: No ToString() and no string concatenation with +
cards/5/explain: The managed collections became native containers, so the data now sits in unmanaged memory that Burst can see. Count turned into Length. Burst builds the message from the literal template and the number itself — no managed string appears. At the interview: “Burst has no managed objects: NativeArray and NativeList instead of T[] and List, FixedString instead of string, and logs are a literal or $"" with primitives.”
cards/6/body:
Burst supports throw only in a simple form — throw new ArgumentException("literal"): the message is embedded in the code statically. What happens next depends on where the code runs:

— in the Editor the exception is forwarded to managed code and printed to the console — it looks like ordinary C#;
— in a player build a throw from Burst code aborts the application. Compiler warning BC1370 tells you exactly that.

That is why checks that throw go into a method marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")]. The symbol is defined in the Editor and not in player builds, so neither the method nor its calls make it into the build. The native containers’ own checks work this way: a clear error in the Editor, zero cost in the build. Safety checks are simply unavailable in player builds, not “off by default”.
cards/6/deep: Two subtleties. If an exception does happen, Burst behaves as if there were no finally blocks — do not rely on finally to release resources on an exception. And if a file has both using UnityEngine; and using System.Diagnostics;, the name Debug becomes ambiguous; then write the attribute in full: [System.Diagnostics.Conditional(...)].
cards/7/q: A Burst job throws ArgumentException when an index is out of range. What does the player see in a release build when that happens?
cards/7/options/0: The application aborts: a throw in Burst code in a player build is an abort
cards/7/options/1: An exception in the log, and the game carries on
cards/7/options/2: Nothing: the build silently skips the throw
cards/7/options/3: The job restarts on the main thread
cards/7/explain: In a player build nothing can catch an exception from Burst code, so the app goes down. To get a clear error in the Editor without crashing the build, put the throwing check in a method marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")].
cards/7/wrong/1: That is the Editor’s behaviour: there the exception is forwarded to managed code. A player build has no such path.
cards/7/wrong/2: Only checks inside [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")] methods vanish from the build, together with the method. An ordinary throw stays and crashes the app.
cards/8/task: In FillJob the count check throws right inside Execute — in a player build that crashes the app. Move the check into static void CheckCount(int count, int length) marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")] and call it from Execute. Keep the message a string literal.
cards/8/checks/0/label: System.Diagnostics is imported (or the attribute is written in full)
cards/8/checks/4/label: There is no throw in Execute
cards/8/explain: In the Editor the check runs and gives a clear exception in the console. In a player build ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS is not defined, so the compiler drops both the method and the call — the throw never reaches native code. The bounds checks inside NativeArray and NativeList work the same way.
cards/9/body:
Polymorphism through classes is not available in Burst, but there are two honest ways around it.

Generics with a struct constraint. If the job is generic over T : struct, IRule, Burst knows the concrete type and calls the method directly: no boxing, no virtual call, and the method can be inlined. The price is a separate copy of the code for each concrete T, and the choice is made at scheduling time, not in the middle of the loop.

FunctionPointer<T> — a pointer to a Burst-compiled static method: the behaviour is chosen at run time. The price is an indirect call that blocks inlining and vectorization (more in unit 3).

But IRule rule = new DoubleRule(); is boxing: the struct is wrapped in a heap object, and Burst code cannot do that.

And the simplest option, which people forget: a switch on an enum field inside a single job.
cards/10/q: Which line will not compile under Burst?
cards/10/explain: object boxed = sum is boxing: the int is wrapped in an object on the managed heap. foreach over a NativeArray is supported, and a FixedString32Bytes field is a fine replacement for a string.
cards/11/q: Interviewer: “A Burst job has to apply one of three behaviour rules. How would you do it?”
cards/11/options/0: A generic job with T : struct, IRule when the rule is known at scheduling time; FunctionPointer<T> when it has to be chosen at run time
cards/11/options/1: An abstract Rule class with a virtual Apply method
cards/11/options/2: A Func<float, float> field in the job struct
cards/11/options/3: A field of type IRule holding the rule struct
cards/11/explain: A generic over a struct gives a direct call with no boxing — the fastest option. FunctionPointer<T> covers the case where the type is not known in advance, at the cost of an indirect call. Another simple route is a switch on an enum inside one job.
cards/11/wrong/1: A class is a managed object, and a virtual call needs an object.
cards/11/wrong/2: A delegate is a managed object; its Burst replacement is FunctionPointer<T>.
cards/11/wrong/3: A struct stored in an interface-typed field is boxing.
